```{r}

#| include: false

Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
data_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),
                                    "../../dev/article-data/plot-sampling"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

We begin with a magnitude-only model to estimate overall tree density in
trees per hectare. Using the [shared simulated forest](plot-sampling-data.html),
we fit the model, examine fitted values, and aggregate predictions for
the forest and its stands. Known population values let us assess parameter
and density estimates. Comparisons with an intercept-only model and
a direct estimate show what canopy height contributes. Subsequent articles
consider composition alone and then combine magnitude and composition to
estimate DBH distributions and species-by-DBH stand tables.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the plot-sampling data (ZIP)](downloads/plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="plot-sampling.zip"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
:::

## Read the data

The shared data use real forest boundaries, plot locations, and UAV-derived
canopy heights from Weisse Krug in Germany [@spitta2026lidar]. Tree
counts are simulated. There are 151 sampled plots and 4,812 prediction cells;
a full plot or cell covers approximately 0.126 ha, with smaller areas along
the forest boundary.

We read the forest polygon and both data tables.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

set.seed(1)

forest <- st_read("data/forest.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
forest_area <- as.numeric(st_area(forest)) / 10000

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, p95, x, count) |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

`count` is the total number of trees, `area` is the sampled area in hectares,
and `p95` is the 95th percentile of canopy-height model values in meters.
The column `x` contains p95 standardized using the plots' mean and standard
deviation. Those same scaling values were applied to the prediction cells.
We fit using the plot counts; simulated prediction-cell counts provide
truth for assessment.

## Define and fit the model

For plot $i$, let $N_i$ be the observed count, $a_i$ its area in hectares,
and $M_i$ the expected tree density in trees per hectare. We relate density
to standardized canopy height $x_i$ and model counts with a negative-binomial
(NB) distribution,

$$
\log M_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad
N_i \mid M_i,r_M \sim \operatorname{NB}(a_i M_i,r_M),
$$

where $a_i M_i$ is the mean count and $r_M$ is the size parameter. Larger
plots have more expected trees at the same density. Count variance is
$a_i M_i + (a_i M_i)^2/r_M$, so a larger size parameter means less variation
around the mean.

The intercept $\beta_0$ is log expected density at the plots' average p95,
and $\beta_1$ describes the change in log density for a one-standard-deviation
increase in p95. In the [technical document](modeling-and-software-details.html), the magnitude
predictors here are $\mathbf z_i=(1,x_i)^\top$.
The data were generated with $\beta_0=\log(350)$,
$\beta_1=-0.2$, and $r_M=50$. These values are known for comparison;
the fit estimates all three parameters.

We supply the counts and areas with `magCompData()`. The formula `~ x`
includes an intercept and a canopy-height slope, while `composition = NULL`
requests a magnitude-only model.

```{r}
#| label: fit

dat <- magCompData(plots, unit = plot_id, tree_count = count,
                   design = fixedArea(area))

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x,
  composition = NULL,
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 2000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) produces parameter draws representing
uncertainty given the data and priors. Each chain runs for 2,000 iterations,
discards the first 1,000, and retains 1,000 draws, giving 3,000 draws across
the three chains. We request three cores to run the chains in parallel and
set their seeds for reproducibility. We use default priors and starting values.
With no magnitude random effects, size is estimated automatically under a Gamma
prior with shape 1 and rate 0.01; its hyperparameters can be changed with
`magCompPriors()`.

### Parameter estimates

We use `summary()` to obtain parameter estimates and diagnostics, then add
the generating values for comparison.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-estimates

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

# Rows are the intercept, standardized p95 slope, and size.
parameter_summary$truth <- c(log(350), -0.2, 50)

parameter_summary |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS")
  )
```

The labels `beta[0]`, `beta[x]`, and `r_M` correspond to $\beta_0$,
$\beta_1$, and $r_M$. The posterior mean summarizes each parameter's draws;
the 2.5% and 97.5% columns bound its central 95% credible interval.
All three generating values fall within these intervals.
Exponentiating a slope draw gives the corresponding multiplicative change
in expected density for a one-standard-deviation increase in p95.

R-hat values near one indicate agreement among chains. ESS is the effective
sample size, accounting for dependence among iterations. We also inspect
the traces: the chains should overlap without a clear upward or downward
trend.

```{r}
#| label: fig-traces
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Retained intercept, canopy-height slope, and size draws. Colors distinguish the three chains."

plot(fit, n_col = 1, n_row = 3)
```

## Examine fitted values

By default, `fitted()` returns posterior means of expected density $M_i$
as `magnitude` and expected count $a_i M_i$ as `count`. We compare these
values with the observed counts at the sampled plots.

```{r}
#| label: fitted-values

fitted_mean <- fitted(fit)

fitted_values <- tibble(
  plot_id = plots$plot_id,
  observed_count = plots$count,
  expected_count = fitted_mean$count[, "total"],
  expected_density = fitted_mean$magnitude[, "total"]
)

fitted_values |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

The table gives counts per plot and densities in trees/ha. We plot observed
counts against fitted mean counts; the dashed line marks equality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted
#| fig-cap: "Observed counts versus fitted mean counts at the 151 sampled plots."

# Use the same count range on both axes, including zero.
count_limits <- range(0, fitted_values$expected_count, fitted_values$observed_count)

ggplot(fitted_values, aes(expected_count, observed_count)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_equal(xlim = count_limits, ylim = count_limits) +
  labs(x = "Fitted mean count", y = "Observed count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Counts vary around their means, so scatter is expected even when the model
is correct. A systematic pattern above or below the line can indicate
underprediction or overprediction. For additional diagnostics,
`ppcSummary(fit)` compares observed counts with posterior predictive
replicates and reports two-sided Bayesian posterior predictive p-values
([Gelman, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1214/13-EJS854)). Small values flag
unusual counts under the model; they are not probabilities that the model
is correct.

## Predict across the forest

To estimate realized forest density, we use posterior predictive counts.
For each selected parameter draw, `target = "observation"` draws a count
from the NB distribution at every prediction cell. This includes count
variation as well as uncertainty in the coefficients and size. The function
returns both these counts and their densities, obtained by dividing by cell
area. We use 100 parameter draws per chain for prediction and retain the
resulting predictive draws for aggregation. The fitted object still holds
all draws for parameter summaries and diagnostics.

```{r}
#| label: predict

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, x, area),
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

# Prediction location x retained draw x chain.
dim(predictions$magnitude)
```

The magnitude array contains 4,812 locations, 100 draws per chain, and
three chains. Each draw uses the same sampled parameters across all
locations. Prediction uses covariates and areas; the simulated cell counts
are reserved for checking the predictions.

We summarize the predictive counts and compare their means with the
simulated counts at these new locations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-predicted
#| fig-cap: "Simulated counts versus posterior predictive mean counts at the 4,812 prediction cells. The dashed line marks equality."

prediction_summary <- summary(predictions) |>
  filter(quantity == "count") |>
  mutate(observed_count = prediction$count)

count_limits <- range(0, prediction_summary$mean, prediction_summary$observed_count)

ggplot(prediction_summary, aes(mean, observed_count)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.3) +
  coord_equal(xlim = count_limits, ylim = count_limits) +
  labs(x = "Predicted mean count", y = "Simulated count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Aggregate with standSummary()

We average predictive densities across cells within each draw. Cell-area
weights give smaller boundary cells less influence.
Omitting `group` in `standSummary()` produces
one summary for the entire forest.

```{r}
#| label: forest-estimate

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)
forest_summary
```

The posterior mean forest density is **`r round(forest_summary$mean, 1)`
trees/ha**, with a 95% posterior predictive interval from
**`r round(forest_summary$q2_5, 1)` to `r round(forest_summary$q97_5, 1)` trees/ha**.
This interval contains the central 95% of the posterior predictive
distribution for forest density. We calculate its endpoints across the
aggregated draws, rather than averaging intervals from individual cells.

To estimate the total number of trees over the forest polygon, multiply each
aggregated density draw by `forest_area` before summarizing. Equivalently,
use `type = "total"` with represented cell areas scaled to sum to `forest_area`.

## Compare with truth and the direct estimate

We calculate the known forest density by applying the same area-weighted
average to simulated cell counts divided by cell area.

```{r}
#| label: forest-truth

true_forest_density <- weighted.mean(
  prediction$count / prediction$area, prediction$area
)
```

To assess the contribution of canopy height, we also fit an intercept-only
model using `~ 1`, predict across the same cells, and aggregate with the same
weights. Both models estimate size and use the same observations, default
priors, and MCMC settings.

```{r}
#| label: intercept-only

intercept_fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ 1,
  composition = NULL,
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 2000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)

intercept_predictions <- predict(
  intercept_fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, area),
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

intercept_forest <- standSummary(
  intercept_predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

intercept_summary <- summary(intercept_forest)
```

We can also compare the model estimates with the design-based direct
estimate, the mean of observed plot densities. We use the usual sample-based
standard error and a Student's t value with 150 degrees of freedom for an
approximate 95% confidence interval. This simple interval calculation does
not account for the systematic arrangement of the inventory plots.

```{r}
#| label: direct-comparison

# Direct estimate and its approximate t-based confidence interval.
sample_density <- plots$count / plots$area
n <- nrow(plots)

direct_mean <- mean(sample_density)
direct_se <- sd(sample_density) / sqrt(n)
direct_interval <- direct_mean + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * direct_se

# Compare the direct estimate and both model estimates.
comparison <- tibble(
  method = c("Direct estimate", "Intercept only", "With canopy height"),
  estimate = c(direct_mean, intercept_summary$mean, forest_summary$mean),
  lower = c(direct_interval[1], intercept_summary$q2_5, forest_summary$q2_5),
  upper = c(direct_interval[2], intercept_summary$q97_5, forest_summary$q97_5)
)

knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Method", "Trees/ha", "Lower 95%", "Upper 95%"))
```

The known forest density is **`r round(true_forest_density, 1)` trees/ha**.
All three estimates use the same 151 sampled plots. Only the model with
canopy height uses predictor information across the forest. We compare
their estimates and intervals with the known density below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-comparison
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Forest density estimates and 95% intervals. Model intervals summarize posterior predictive draws; the direct estimate has an approximate Student's t confidence interval. The dashed line marks simulated truth."

ggplot(comparison, aes(method, estimate, color = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_forest_density, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.15) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Direct estimate" = "#D55E00",
                                "Intercept only" = "#009E73",
                                "With canopy height" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Forest density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Here the intercept-only estimate is close to the direct estimate. Adding
canopy height brings the forest estimate closer to truth and gives a somewhat
narrower interval. The canopy-height model accounts for differences in the
predictor distribution between sampled plots and the forest grid.

A design-based confidence interval is interpreted through repeated sampling
from the same forest. The model interval assigns 95% posterior probability
to the stated range for forest density, conditional on the observations,
model, and priors. Their widths need not agree, and adding a predictor does
not guarantee a narrower interval.

## Estimate stand densities

The same predictions also give density estimates for each of the 249 stands.
Some cells cross stand boundaries, so we use the area of each cell within
each stand as its weight. A cell contributes the same predicted density draw
to every stand it overlaps.

We read the overlap table constructed in the [data article](plot-sampling-data.html#cell-areas-within-stands).
In `standSummary()`, `unit` identifies the prediction cell, `group` identifies
the stand, and `represented_area` gives its area within that stand. The
function averages densities within each stand for every posterior draw.

```{r}
#| label: stand-estimates

cell_stand_areas <- read_csv("data/cell_stand_areas.csv")

stand_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = cell_stand_areas,
  unit = prediction_id,
  group = stand_id,
  represented_area = area_ha,
  summary = "samples"
)

stand_estimates <- summary(stand_predictions) |>
  transmute(stand_id = unit, estimate = mean, lower = q2_5, upper = q97_5)
```

We calculate true stand densities from the simulated cell counts using the
same overlap areas, then compare estimates and their 95% posterior predictive
intervals with truth. The dashed line marks equality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stand-estimates
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true stand density. Points are posterior means and vertical bars are 95% posterior predictive intervals for the 249 stands."

stand_truth <- cell_stand_areas |>
  left_join(
    prediction |> transmute(prediction_id = plot_id, density = count / area),
    by = "prediction_id"
  ) |>
  group_by(stand_id) |>
  summarise(truth = weighted.mean(density, area_ha), .groups = "drop")

stand_estimates <- stand_estimates |>
  left_join(stand_truth, by = "stand_id")

stand_limits <- range(0, stand_estimates$truth, stand_estimates$lower,
                       stand_estimates$upper)

ggplot(stand_estimates, aes(truth, estimate)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                 color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 1.5) +
  coord_equal(xlim = stand_limits, ylim = stand_limits) +
  labs(x = "True stand density (trees/ha)",
       y = "Estimated stand density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The model gives estimates for stands with and without sampled plots because
canopy height is available across the forest. Each interval summarizes the
aggregated predictive draws for that stand.

to describe how a known total is allocated among species.
